content.text: A subagent isn't a clone of your session. Unless it's a fork, it starts with a fresh context window: its own instructions, usually your CLAUDE.md, and one task message that Claude writes for it. Nothing you and Claude decided in the conversation reaches it unless that message says so. Brief it like a new teammate: the goal, what's settled, where to look, what to skip and what to send back.
You've spent an hour with Claude on a flaky HTTP client. Together you've established that the bug is in the retry loop, not the cache, that
fetchWithRetry
must keep its public signature because two other teams call it, and that
vendor/
is generated. You type "use a subagent to review my changes". The review comes back with three findings: change the signature of
fetchWithRetry
, add a response cache, and fix the formatting in
vendor/
. Every one of them is something the conversation already settled. The reviewer wasn't there for any of it.
The common misconception
"A subagent is a copy of the current session, so it already knows everything we've discussed." It's easy to see why:

items.text: It runs inside your session, starts from your prompt and works on the same repository.
Claude starts it, and Claude clearly knows the context, so it seems natural that the context comes along.
Since fork mode became the default, Claude can start forks, which really do inherit the whole conversation.
The results come back sounding confident and fluent, so a missing piece of background is easy to miss.

content.text: The half-truth is the fork. A fork does carry your conversation. But the Explore agent Claude uses for broad searches, the general-purpose agent, your custom subagents and skills that run with
context: fork
all start fresh.
What actually happens
A fresh context window, on purpose
The docs are explicit: each
subagent
"starts with a fresh, isolated context window. It doesn't see your conversation history, the skills you've already invoked, or the files Claude has already read." What it does start with is short:

items.text: Its own system prompt, not the Claude Code system prompt
The task message Claude writes when it hands off the work
Your CLAUDE.md files and a git status snapshot, except for the built-in Explore and Plan agents, which skip both
The full text of any skills its definition preloads

content.text: Your output style and auto memory don't reach it either. That isolation is the point. The subagent can read fifty files in its own
context window
and hand back a summary, and none of those reads fill yours.
The task message is the whole briefing

"Claude composes a delegation message that summarizes the task, and the subagent works from there." Even when you @-mention a specific subagent, your full message goes to Claude, which writes the subagent's prompt from what you asked. So your words shape the brief. "Review my changes" becomes a brief with no decisions in it, and a reviewer with no decisions to respect.
Forks are the exception
A
fork

inherits the whole conversation: the same system prompt, tools, model and history. Because its first request matches the parent's, it reuses the parent's prompt cache, so it costs less than a fresh subagent for a task that needs the same context. You can start one yourself with
/subtask
followed by the task.
Don't confuse it with a skill's
context: fork
setting. Despite the name, such a skill runs in a fresh subagent that "doesn't see your conversation history", so its instructions have to stand on their own.

rows.text: Side tasks that need the history
Focused work, a reviewer with fresh eyes

content.text: Only the result comes back

The subagent's own tool calls stay out of your conversation; its final result is what returns. That cuts both ways. Ask for a long report and you get a long report in your context. Run several subagents in parallel that each return details, and the docs warn that they "can consume significant context".
The same delegation, briefed two ways

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code: use a subagent to review my changes

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
Use a subagent to review my diff in src/http/ (git diff main).
It can't see our chat, so tell it: fetchWithRetry's signature
stays (other teams call it), and caching is ruled out.
Check that every caller handles TimeoutError and that retries
stop at 3. Skip vendor/ (generated) and style. Return at most
10 findings, each as file:line plus one sentence.

content.text: The second prompt costs a minute and carries everything the reviewer can't infer: the goal, the decisions, what to skip and the size of the answer. It also keeps what makes a fresh reviewer valuable. The docs point out that a reviewer who didn't write the code "isn't swayed by the reasoning that produced the code"; you want it to know your constraints, not your conclusions.
When you brief the same kind of worker every week, move the standing parts into a definition in
.claude/agents/
. The body becomes the subagent's system prompt:

blocks.code:
---
name: http-reviewer
description: Reviews changes to src/http/. Use after edits there.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
---
You review a diff you didn't write, with no chat history.
- Public signatures in src/http/index.ts are frozen.
- Ignore vendor/ (generated) and formatting.
Report at most 10 findings as file:line plus one sentence.
If you find nothing, say so; don't invent issues.

blocks.title: Restate the rules that must reach it

content.text: The main conversation still has your full CLAUDE.md when it reads a subagent's results, so most rules don't need to reach the subagent. When one must, such as "ignore the vendor/ directory", the docs' advice is to restate it in the prompt you give Claude when delegating, especially for Explore and Plan, which skip CLAUDE.md.

blocks.title: A subagent isn't a smarter answer

content.text: By default it's the same model, or a smaller one, on the same task, and every subagent sends its own requests against your usage. A fresh one first has to rediscover context your conversation already had, so it can be slower than doing the work in place. Use subagents for parallel work, noisy output and fresh eyes, not for a better answer.
How to apply it in your project
If the task needs the history, fork it with
/subtask
. If it needs independence, such as a review, use a fresh subagent.
Say the goal, what's decided or ruled out, where to look, what to skip and which tools or commands to use.
Ask for a format and a limit, such as ten findings as file:line, so the result doesn't flood your context.
Put repeated instructions, a tool list and the output format in
.claude/agents/<name>.md
, and keep the description short.
Run
/usage
to see what share each subagent type takes, and set
model: haiku
for simple jobs like collecting files.
Key takeaways

items.text: A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context window, not a copy of your session.
The task message Claude writes is the whole briefing, so what you ask shapes what it knows.
Explore and Plan also skip CLAUDE.md; restate rules they must follow.
A fork inherits the conversation; a skill's
Brief for the goal, the decisions, the scope and the size of the answer.
